title: Community Nutrition and Food Security
subtitle: Measure your household's diet, feed young children well, and lead a practical, measurable nutrition improvement in your community using local foods.
description: A practical course on closing the gap between enough food and the right food. You learn the four pillars of food security and the forms of malnutrition, score diets with the food groups used by FAO, WHO and UNICEF, apply infant feeding and food safety guidance, screen and refer children correctly, and build a measured 90-day community plan.
outcomes: Explain food security and the main forms of malnutrition in plain language
Score a person's diet with the 10 food groups and track it week by week
Plan safe, enriched first foods and meals for children aged 6 to 23 months
Store food safely, prevent mould and handle leftovers within safe time limits
Recognise MUAC and oedema warning signs and refer a child to the right service
Write and deliver a 90-day nutrition plan with SMART goals, indicators and partners
audience: Women who feed families and want to improve nutrition at home and lead simple, safe nutrition action in their community, with no prior health training.
tools: A notebook and pen, or a phone with a notes or spreadsheet app
A phone camera for evidence photos
Access to a local market for price checks
Optional: woven sacks or buckets, soil and seeds for a kitchen garden
Optional: a MUAC tape, only after training by a health worker

modules.title: Food Security and Malnutrition: Seeing the Real Problem
modules.overview: You learn what food security really means, the different faces of malnutrition, and how local Nigerian foods fit into food groups. You finish the module with an honest picture of your own household and community, measured with a simple dietary diversity score and a seasonal calendar.

lessons.title: Full stomach, hidden hunger: food security and the forms of malnutrition
objectives: Explain food security using its four parts: availability, access, utilisation and stability
Tell the difference between stunting, wasting, underweight, micronutrient deficiency and overweight
Describe how poor diet and infection feed each other in a cycle
Explain why the first 1,000 days matter most

blocks.text: A child can eat three times a day and still be malnourished. If every meal is mostly garri, white rice or pap with little beans, fish, egg or vegetables, the stomach is full but the body is missing protein, iron, vitamin A, zinc and iodine. Health workers call this **hidden hunger**. This course is about closing the gap between enough food and the right food, at home and in your community.

blocks.name: family
blocks.caption: Food security is a household and community matter: every member, every season.

blocks.text: What food security means

The definition used by FAO and governments since the 1996 World Food Summit says food security exists when all people, at all times, have physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food that meets their dietary needs and food preferences for an active and healthy life. That long sentence breaks into four parts, sometimes called the four pillars.

head: Pillar
Plain question
Local example of a problem
rows: Is the food there at all?
Tomatoes and leafy vegetables are scarce in the dry season, or a flood destroys the harvest
Can the family get it, with money, farm or gifts?
Beans are in the market but the family cannot afford them this month
Does the body actually use the food well?
Dirty water causes repeated diarrhoea, so the child loses nutrients; or food is overcooked and badly shared
Is it steady through the year and through shocks?
Food is fine after harvest but runs out between May and August, or prices jump suddenly

blocks.text: Notice that only one pillar is about whether food exists. Many families in Nigerian towns live near busy markets, so availability is fine, yet access is the problem because prices rose faster than income. Utilisation is often forgotten: clean water, handwashing, good cooking and fair sharing inside the home decide whether food becomes nutrition.
The different faces of malnutrition

WHO groups malnutrition into undernutrition, micronutrient problems, and overweight with diet-related diseases. Health workers use three body measures for children under five. Each compares the child with the WHO Child Growth Standards for a healthy child of the same age and sex.

items: **Stunting**: too short for age. It builds slowly from months of poor diet and repeated illness, often starting in pregnancy. It is linked to poorer learning and is hard to reverse after about age two.
**Wasting**: too thin for height. It can develop quickly after illness or food shortage and is dangerous; severe wasting raises the risk of death and needs urgent treatment.
**Underweight**: low weight for age. It can reflect stunting, wasting or both, and is what the weight line on a child health card shows.
**Micronutrient deficiency**: lack of vitamins and minerals such as iron, vitamin A, iodine and zinc, even when weight looks fine.
**Overweight and obesity**: too much energy, often from sugary drinks, fried snacks and refined starch, which raises the risk of diabetes and high blood pressure later.

blocks.text: One household can carry more than one problem at the same time: a stunted child and an overweight parent eating the same cheap, starchy, oily diet. This is called the **double burden of malnutrition**, and it is why the answer is never just more food. The answer is more variety.

blocks.title: The malnutrition and infection cycle
items: Poor diet
Weaker immunity
More infections
Less appetite, nutrients lost
Poorer nutrition
blocks.caption: Each turn of the cycle makes the next one worse, so breaking it at any point (food, clean water, vaccination, early treatment) helps.

blocks.text: A child with diarrhoea or measles eats less, absorbs less and uses more energy fighting the illness. She comes out of each illness thinner, and a thinner child catches the next infection more easily. That is why community nutrition work always includes clean water, handwashing, immunisation and quick treatment of illness, not only food.
Why the first 1,000 days matter

The period from pregnancy to a child's second birthday is called the **first 1,000 days**. The brain and body grow fastest then, so the effects of good or poor nutrition are largest and longest lasting. A pregnant woman's diet, breastfeeding, and the first foods a baby eats from six months are the most valuable targets for your effort.

blocks.title: Worked example: naming the real problem
blocks.context: For example, Halima in a town near Kano feeds her family of six. They eat tuwo or rice twice a day with a thin soup, and there is enough to feel full. Her 20-month-old son is shorter than his cousins of the same age, and her husband has been told his blood pressure is high.
steps: Availability: food is in the market all year, so this is not the main problem.
Access: she can afford some beans and fish but buys mostly grain because it fills more stomachs per naira.
Utilisation: the soup has little vegetable or protein, and the toddler often has diarrhoea from untreated well water.
Forms of malnutrition: the boy shows signs of stunting; the father's diet is high in salt, oil and refined starch.
Cycle: repeated diarrhoea plus a low-variety diet keeps the boy in the malnutrition and infection cycle.
blocks.result: Halima's household has a double burden and an access plus utilisation problem. Her best first steps are safer drinking water, more beans and leafy vegetables in the soup, and taking the toddler to the clinic for growth measurement, not simply buying more grain.

blocks.title: When to go to a clinic today
blocks.text: A child who is very thin, has swelling of both feet, refuses to eat or drink, is unusually sleepy, or has diarrhoea with signs of dehydration needs a health facility the same day. Food advice is not a substitute for treatment.

takeaways: Food security has four pillars: availability, access, utilisation and stability
Stunting is too short for age, wasting is too thin for height, underweight is low weight for age
Poor diet and infection feed each other, so water, hygiene and treatment are part of nutrition
The first 1,000 days, from pregnancy to age two, are the most important window

activity.title: Name your household's pillars
steps: Draw a table with the four pillars as rows.
For each pillar, write one honest sentence about your household this month.
Circle the pillar that causes the most trouble.
List every child under five and every pregnant or breastfeeding woman in the home.
Write which of them you will focus on first, and why.
activity.evidence: A photo of your four-pillar table with the weakest pillar circled

lessons.title: Local foods that do the most work: food groups, nutrients and value for money
objectives: Sort common Nigerian foods into the 10 food groups used to measure diet quality
Name local sources of iron, vitamin A, iodine and protein
Calculate the cost per gram of protein for different foods
Combine foods so the body absorbs more iron

blocks.text: In school many of us learned three groups: energy-giving foods, body-building foods and protective foods. That is a good start, but it hides an important point: a meal with rice, a little stew and one slice of tomato ticks all three boxes yet is still poor. Nutrition workers now use a more detailed list of food groups to check whether a diet is varied enough.

blocks.name: leafy-green
blocks.alt: A bunch of dark green leafy vegetables
blocks.caption: Dark green leaves such as ugu, efo tete and moringa are among the cheapest nutrient-rich foods in our markets.

blocks.text: The 10 food groups

FAO's Minimum Dietary Diversity for Women (MDD-W) indicator uses 10 groups. A woman who ate foods from at least 5 of the 10 groups yesterday is much more likely to be getting enough vitamins and minerals. We will use the same list for the whole family in this course.

head: Food group
Nigerian examples
rows: Rice, maize, millet, sorghum, acha, yam, cassava, garri, white sweet potato, plantain
Beans (cowpea), soybeans, bambara nut, pigeon pea
Fresh milk, nono, wara, yoghurt, powdered milk
Chicken, goat, beef, liver, fresh or dried fish, crayfish, snails
Chicken, duck or guinea fowl eggs
Ugu, efo tete (amaranth), waterleaf, bitter leaf, moringa, sweet potato leaves
8. Other vitamin A-rich fruits and vegetables
Ripe mango, pawpaw, carrot, orange-fleshed sweet potato, yellow-fleshed pumpkin
Tomato, onion, okra, garden egg, cucumber, cabbage
Orange, banana, pineapple, watermelon, guava, African star apple (agbalumo)

blocks.text: Red palm oil is not one of the 10 groups, because oils are counted separately, but it is worth knowing: unrefined red palm oil is rich in carotenoids that the body turns into vitamin A. Using it in moderation in soups and stews is a traditional strength of many Nigerian diets.
Four nutrients to watch

items: **Iron** prevents anaemia, which causes tiredness and poor concentration. Best absorbed from liver, meat, fish and crayfish; also found in beans and leafy greens.
**Vitamin A** protects eyesight and helps fight infection. Found in liver, egg yolk, red palm oil, dark green leaves, mango, pawpaw and orange-fleshed sweet potato.
**Iodine** is needed for the brain and thyroid. The simplest source is iodised salt; keep it covered and away from heat so the iodine is not lost.
**Protein** builds and repairs the body. Beans, groundnuts, eggs, fish, milk and meat all provide it, and mixing a grain with a pulse (rice and beans, moi moi with pap) gives better quality protein.

blocks.title: Pair foods to absorb more iron
blocks.text: Vitamin C helps the body absorb the iron in beans and leaves. Eat orange, guava, pawpaw or tomato with the meal. Tea, coffee and some cocoa drinks reduce iron absorption, so take them between meals rather than with food.
Preparation that keeps the goodness

How you prepare food changes what the body receives. Soaking beans overnight and throwing away the soaking water shortens cooking time and makes them easier to digest. Fermenting maize into ogi, or sprouting grains, helps release minerals such as iron and zinc. Leafy vegetables lose vitamin C when boiled for a long time, so add ugu or efo near the end of cooking and cut them just before use rather than hours earlier.
Value for money: cost per gram of protein

When money is tight, compare foods by what they give the body, not by the price per bag. The worked example below uses rough protein values (about 23 g of protein per 100 g of dry beans, about 25 g per 100 g of groundnuts, about 6 g per egg) and example prices. Prices change often, so redo the sums with your own market prices.

blocks.title: Worked example: which protein gives the most for the money?
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi in Enugu has example prices (approximate, check your market): 1 kg of beans for 3,000 naira, 1 kg of groundnuts for 3,200 naira, and a crate of 30 eggs for 7,500 naira.
steps: Beans: 1 kg = 1,000 g, so protein is about 1,000 x 23 / 100 = 230 g. Cost per gram = 3,000 / 230 = about 13 naira.
Groundnuts: protein is about 1,000 x 25 / 100 = 250 g. Cost per gram = 3,200 / 250 = about 12.8 naira.
Eggs: 30 x 6 g = 180 g of protein. Cost per gram = 7,500 / 180 = about 42 naira.
She notes that eggs cost more per gram but give vitamin A, B12 and very high quality protein, and are easy to feed to a baby.
blocks.result: Beans and groundnuts give protein at about one third of the cost of eggs. Ngozi makes beans and groundnut the daily base, and buys a few eggs each week mainly for her one-year-old and her pregnant sister.

blocks.title: Where to spend the food budget
items: Cheap and nutrient-rich: buy daily
Costly and nutrient-rich: buy for priority members
Cheap but low nutrients: fill, then add
Costly and low nutrients: cut first
blocks.caption: Beans, leaves and groundnuts sit top-left; sugary drinks and packaged snacks belong bottom-right and are the first to cut.

blocks.text: Sugary drinks, sweets and packaged snacks often eat a surprising share of the food budget. One bottle of soft drink a day across a month can cost as much as several kilograms of beans. Cutting those first frees money for the top-left box without spending more in total.

takeaways: Use the 10 food groups to judge variety; aim for at least 5 groups a day
Leafy greens, beans, groundnuts and red palm oil are low-cost nutrient powerhouses
Eat vitamin C foods with iron foods; keep tea and coffee away from meals
Compare protein foods by cost per gram, not by bag price
Use iodised salt and store it covered

activity.title: Market value check
steps: Visit your nearest market or shop, or ask a trusted seller by phone.
Write today's price for 1 kg of beans, 1 kg of groundnuts, one egg and one portion of fish.
Calculate cost per gram of protein for beans, groundnuts and eggs using the values in this lesson.
List three local foods in groups 7 and 8 (leafy greens and vitamin A-rich foods) and their prices.
Write one item you will cut from the bottom-right box to pay for a top-left food.
activity.evidence: Your price list with the three cost-per-gram calculations

lessons.title: Your starting point: diet score, seasonal calendar and community food map
objectives: Record a 24-hour food recall and calculate a dietary diversity score
Draw a seasonal calendar showing the lean months and price peaks
Map where your community gets food and what support already exists
Choose one specific nutrition gap to work on

blocks.text: Good advice starts with good facts about your own situation. In this lesson you will measure three things: what your household actually ate, how food changes through the year, and what your community already has. Together they become your baseline, the starting point you will compare against at the end of the course.

blocks.name: checklist
blocks.alt: A person ticking items on a large checklist
blocks.caption: A simple food-group tick list turns 'we eat well' into a number you can track.

blocks.text: Tool 1: the 24-hour recall and diversity score

items: Choose one person (start with yourself or the youngest child above six months).
Ask about everything eaten or drunk from waking yesterday to waking today: meals, snacks, drinks, and food eaten outside the home.
For mixed dishes, list the ingredients. Egusi soup may contain egusi, ugu, palm oil, crayfish and meat.
Tick each of the 10 food groups that appears. Very small amounts used only for flavour, such as a pinch of crayfish powder, are usually not counted.
Count the ticked groups. That number out of 10 is the dietary diversity score. For women, 5 or more is the target.

blocks.title: Worked example: scoring a day
blocks.context: For example, Amina in Ilorin recalls yesterday: pap with sugar in the morning, rice and tomato stew with a small piece of fish at lunch, garri soaked with water and groundnuts in the evening, and one orange.
steps: Pap (maize) and rice and garri: group 1, grains and roots. Tick.
Tomato in the stew: group 9, other vegetables. Tick.
Fish: group 5, meat, poultry and fish. Tick.
Groundnuts: group 3, nuts and seeds. Tick.
Orange: group 10, other fruits. Tick.
No beans, dairy, eggs, leafy greens or vitamin A-rich fruit: groups 2, 4, 6, 7 and 8 missing.
blocks.result: Amina scores 5 out of 10, just at the target, but she has no dark leafy greens or vitamin A-rich foods. Adding ugu to the stew and a slice of ripe pawpaw would lift her to 7 at little cost.

blocks.text: One day can be unusual, so repeat the recall on three different days, including one market day and one non-market day, and take the average. Write the scores down; you will use them again in Module 2.
Tool 2: the seasonal calendar

In much of Nigeria, the months before the main harvest are the hardest. Stored grain runs low, prices rise, and farm work is heavy. Many people call this the lean season or hunger gap. The timing differs by region and by crop, so draw your own calendar instead of copying someone else's.

blocks.title: A seasonal food calendar (fill in your own months)
items: Harvest: food plentiful, prices low
Dry season: fewer fresh vegetables
Planting: money spent on seeds
Lean months: stores low, prices high
Early harvest: green maize, relief
blocks.caption: Mark your own months under each stage, then plan storage and gardens to cover the lean months.

blocks.text: Ask two or three older women in your area to help. For each month, note which foods are cheap, which are scarce, when school fees or farm costs fall, and when illnesses such as malaria and diarrhoea are common. Problems that pile up in the same months show you where to act first.
Tool 3: the community food map

items: Food sources: markets, shops, farms, fishing points, and where people buy cooked food.
Water sources: which are protected (borehole, treated tap) and which are not (open well, stream).
Health support: the nearest primary health care centre, its immunisation and growth monitoring days, and community health workers.
Farming support: agricultural extension officers, cooperatives, and seed or seedling sellers.
Groups: women's associations, religious groups, savings groups and school PTAs that could carry a nutrition message.

blocks.text: Warning signs of food stress

Food programmes such as WFP watch how families cope when food runs short, because the coping itself is a warning sign. Ask yourself, and later your neighbours, how many days in the last week the household had to do any of the following. The more days, and the more serious the step, the deeper the food insecurity.

head: Coping step
What it tells you
rows: Early stress: variety is dropping first
Borrowing food or buying on credit
Quantity is now short as well as quality
Adults eating less so children can eat
Mothers are often the first to go without, which harms pregnancy and breastfeeding
Skipping whole meals or selling tools and animals
Serious stress: the household is using up its future to eat today

blocks.title: Respect privacy
blocks.text: When you ask neighbours about what they ate or how much they spend, explain why, ask permission, and never share names or answers in group chats. Food shortage can be a source of shame. Record households by a number, not a name.

Finally, put the three tools together and choose one specific gap. A gap is specific when it names who, what and when, for example: 'my two children rarely eat dark leafy greens or eggs, worst from June to August'. That sentence will guide the rest of your course.

takeaways: A 24-hour recall with the 10 food groups gives a dietary diversity score; 5 or more is the target for women
Average at least three days before drawing conclusions
A seasonal calendar shows when food, money and illness problems pile up
Map existing food, water, health and farming support before starting anything new
End with one specific gap: who, what and when

activity.title: Build your baseline
steps: Do a 24-hour recall for yourself and one child on three different days.
Calculate each day's score and the average for each person.
Draw a 12-month seasonal calendar with at least one older community member.
Sketch a simple map of food, water, health and farming points near you.
Write your specific gap in one sentence: who, what and when.
activity.evidence: Baseline sheet with three recall scores per person, the seasonal calendar photo, and your one-sentence gap

quiz.q: A family in Lagos lives beside a busy market but cannot afford beans or fish since prices rose. Which pillar of food security is weakest?
quiz.explain: The food is there (availability), but the family cannot obtain it with their money. That is an access problem.

quiz.q: A health worker says a child is 'too thin for his height'. Which term describes this?
quiz.explain: Wasting is low weight for height. Stunting is low height for age.

quiz.q: Yesterday Bola ate pap, rice with tomato stew and chicken, and a banana. What is her dietary diversity score using the 10 groups?
quiz.explain: Grains (pap, rice), other vegetables (tomato), meat and poultry (chicken), other fruits (banana): 4 groups.

quiz.q: Beans cost 2,760 naira per kg in a market (example price). With about 23 g protein per 100 g, what is the cost per gram of protein?
quiz.explain: 1 kg gives about 230 g protein. 2,760 / 230 = 12 naira per gram.

quiz.q: Which habit helps the body absorb more iron from a bean and ugu meal?
options: Eating an orange or guava with the meal
Boiling the vegetables for a long time
quiz.explain: Vitamin C in orange or guava increases absorption of iron from plant foods. Tea reduces it.

quiz.q: Why does community nutrition work include clean water and handwashing?
options: Because infections like diarrhoea reduce appetite and nutrient absorption, worsening malnutrition
Because it replaces the need for vegetables
Because clean water prevents stunting on its own
quiz.explain: Infection and poor diet form a cycle. Preventing infection protects the nutrition the child gets from food.

modules.title: Field Practice: Feeding, Food Safety and Measuring Change
modules.overview: This module gives you the practical tools community nutrition workers use: infant and young child feeding practice, safe preparation and storage of food, and simple measurements (growth cards, MUAC screening and diet scores) that show whether things are improving.

lessons.title: Feeding the first 1,000 days: pregnancy, breastfeeding and first foods
objectives: Explain WHO recommendations for breastfeeding from birth to two years
Plan the texture, amount and number of meals for a baby aged 6 to 23 months
Enrich a local pap or porridge so it covers at least 5 of 8 food groups
Describe extra food needs for pregnant and breastfeeding women

blocks.text: If you can only change one thing in your community, change how babies and young children are fed. WHO and UNICEF guidance, followed by Nigeria's Federal Ministry of Health, is clear and simple. This lesson turns it into practical steps with local foods.

blocks.name: motherhood
blocks.caption: Breastfeeding and good first foods are the strongest protection in the first 1,000 days.

blocks.text: Birth to six months: breast milk only

items: Put the baby to the breast within **one hour of birth**. The first thick yellow milk, colostrum, is rich in antibodies; do not throw it away.

Give **only breast milk for the first six months**: no water, glucose water, herbal drinks, pap or formula unless a health worker advises it for a medical reason. Breast milk contains enough water even in hot weather.
Feed on demand, day and night. Frequent feeding keeps the milk supply up.
Continue breastfeeding **up to two years or beyond** while other foods are added.

blocks.text: From six months: first foods

At about six months, breast milk alone no longer covers a baby's needs for energy, iron and zinc. WHO advises starting small amounts of food and increasing gradually: 2 to 3 meals a day at 6 to 8 months, and 3 to 4 meals a day at 9 to 23 months, with 1 to 2 nutritious snacks if the child is hungry. The table uses a 250 ml cup, about the size of a standard plastic drinking cup.

head: Age
Texture
Amount per meal
Meals a day
rows: Thick porridge or well-mashed food, thick enough to stay on a tilted spoon
Start with 2 to 3 tablespoons, slowly increase to half a 250 ml cup
Finely chopped or mashed family food, soft finger foods
Three quarters to a full 250 ml cup

blocks.title: Feeding stages from birth to two years
items: Birth: breastfeed within one hour
0 to 6 months: breast milk only
6 to 8 months: thick first foods
9 to 11 months: chopped food, snacks
12 to 23 months: family food, keep breastfeeding
blocks.caption: Each stage adds food while breastfeeding continues, never replacing it before two years.

blocks.text: Variety: at least 5 of 8 groups

For children aged 6 to 23 months, WHO and UNICEF measure **minimum dietary diversity** with 8 groups: breast milk; grains, roots, tubers and plantain; pulses, nuts and seeds; dairy; flesh foods (meat, fish, poultry, liver); eggs; vitamin A-rich fruits and vegetables; and other fruits and vegetables. A child who ate from at least 5 of these 8 groups yesterday meets the target. Plain pap made from maize or millet alone covers only one group, which is why it must be enriched.

blocks.title: Worked example: enriching ogi for an 8-month-old
blocks.context: For example, Chiamaka in Owerri gives her 8-month-old daughter plain ogi with a little sugar twice a day, plus breast milk. The baby's diet scores 2 of 8 (breast milk and grains).
steps: She makes the ogi thicker so it stays on a tilted spoon, instead of a thin drink.
Into about half a 250 ml cup of ogi she stirs 1 tablespoon of smooth groundnut paste (pulses, nuts and seeds).
She adds 1 teaspoon of finely ground crayfish, checked for grit and sand (flesh foods).
At lunch she mashes a soft-boiled egg into yam or rice (eggs), and gives mashed ripe pawpaw as a snack (vitamin A-rich fruit).
She drops the added sugar, since the groundnut and fruit already make the food tasty.
blocks.result: The baby now eats from breast milk, grains, nuts, flesh foods, eggs and vitamin A-rich fruit: 6 of 8 groups, above the target, at a modest extra cost.

blocks.title: Baby food safety
blocks.text: Wash hands with soap before preparing food and before feeding. Use a clean cup and spoon, not a feeding bottle, which is hard to clean. Grind groundnuts into smooth paste, because whole nuts can choke a young child. Do not give honey before the first birthday. Avoid sweet drinks, tea and coffee for young children, and feed freshly made food rather than food kept for hours.
Responsive feeding and the sick child

Sit with the child, talk to her, and watch for signs of hunger and fullness. Encourage, but never force or threaten. Give the child her own plate so you can see how much she ate. When a child is ill, keep breastfeeding and offer small, frequent meals and fluids; after the illness, offer more food than usual for some time to help her catch up. Children with diarrhoea should be taken to a health worker for oral rehydration salts and zinc as advised.
Mothers need extra food too

Pregnant and breastfeeding women need more energy and nutrients. WHO and UNICEF counselling materials commonly advise about one extra small meal or snack a day during pregnancy and two while breastfeeding, from varied foods. Pregnant women should attend antenatal care early, where the clinic provides iron and folic acid supplements; take them exactly as the health worker directs. Use iodised salt, and make sure the mother is not the one who always eats last and least.

takeaways: Breastfeed within one hour, exclusively for six months, and continue to two years or beyond
From six months add thick, enriched foods: 2 to 3 meals at 6 to 8 months, 3 to 4 from 9 months
Aim for at least 5 of 8 food groups for children aged 6 to 23 months
Use clean cups and spoons, grind nuts, no honey before one year
Pregnant and breastfeeding women need extra meals and antenatal care

activity.title: Design a day of food for a young child
steps: Choose a real child aged 6 to 23 months in your home or community (with the mother's permission).
Write what the child ate yesterday and score it out of the 8 groups.
Plan one day of meals and snacks that reaches at least 5 groups, using the table for amounts.
Prepare one enriched porridge and photograph it.
Ask the mother what was easy and what was hard, and note it.
activity.evidence: A one-day feeding plan with group score before and after, plus a photo of the enriched porridge

lessons.title: Safe food, safe storage and fair sharing at home
objectives: Apply the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food in a home kitchen
Store grain and legumes to prevent mould and weevils
Handle leftovers using safe times and temperatures
Check that food is shared fairly among household members

blocks.text: Food that is contaminated, mouldy or badly shared does not become good nutrition. This lesson covers the utilisation pillar: keeping food safe from farm to plate and making sure the people who need it most actually get it.

blocks.name: wash-hands
blocks.alt: A person washing hands at a sink
blocks.caption: Washing hands with soap and safe water is the first of the WHO Five Keys.

blocks.text: The WHO Five Keys to Safer Food

blocks.title: WHO Five Keys to Safer Food
items: Keep clean
Separate raw and cooked
Cook thoroughly
Keep food at safe temperatures
Use safe water and raw materials
blocks.caption: These five habits prevent most foodborne illness in homes and food businesses.

items: **Keep clean**: wash hands with soap before handling food and after using the toilet or changing a nappy; keep surfaces, pots and cloths clean; cover food from flies.
**Separate raw and cooked**: keep raw meat, fish and their juices away from cooked food and fruit; use a separate knife and board, or wash them well between uses.
**Cook thoroughly**: cook meat, chicken, eggs and fish until juices run clear and there is no pink; bring soups and stews to the boil when reheating.
**Keep food at safe temperatures**: do not leave cooked food at room temperature for more than 2 hours; keep it hot (above 60 degrees C) or cold (below 5 degrees C); reheat until steaming hot.
**Use safe water and raw materials**: use boiled or treated water; choose fresh, undamaged food; wash fruits and vegetables, especially if eaten raw; do not use food after its expiry date.

blocks.title: Worked example: leftovers after a naming ceremony
blocks.context: For example, Ruth in Ibadan cooked jollof rice and chicken stew that were ready at 1 pm. Guests left at 5 pm. She has no fridge, but there is light most evenings at her neighbour's house.
steps: Time at room temperature: from 1 pm to 5 pm is 4 hours, double the 2-hour limit.
The rice has been sitting warm for 4 hours. Cooked rice left warm can grow bacteria whose toxins are not destroyed by reheating, so she does not keep it for the children.
For the next event she plans ahead: she will keep stew in the pot on a low fire, above 60 degrees C, and serve rice in batches.
Any portion she wants to keep will be cooled in shallow bowls and taken to the neighbour's fridge within 2 hours of cooking.
Kept stew will be boiled again until it bubbles before eating the next day.
blocks.result: Ruth throws away the rice left out for 4 hours instead of risking diarrhoea in her children, and writes a simple plan so that next time no food sits out beyond 2 hours.

blocks.text: Safe drinking water at home

Water from open wells, streams and some boreholes can carry germs that cause diarrhoea, which steals nutrients from children. If you are not sure your water is safe, bring it to a rolling boil, let it cool covered, and store it in a clean container with a lid and a tap, or pour it out rather than dipping cups and hands inside. Water for preparing baby food and mixing oral rehydration salts must always be safe water.
Storing grain, beans and groundnuts

Moulds that grow on damp or damaged maize, groundnuts and other grains can produce **aflatoxins**, poisons that you cannot see, smell or cook away. Long-term exposure is linked to liver damage, and in children to poor growth. Prevention is all about dryness and sorting.

items: Dry grain and legumes well before storing. A simple check: put a handful of grain and two spoons of dry salt in a dry, clear bottle, close and shake for a minute. If salt sticks to the sides, the grain is still too damp.
Sort and remove mouldy, shrivelled, discoloured or insect-damaged grains and nuts. Throw them away; do not sell them or feed them to animals.
Store in clean, airtight containers or hermetic (airtight) storage bags, such as triple-layer PICS bags widely used for cowpeas. Without air, weevils die without chemicals.
Keep sacks off the floor on wooden pallets and away from walls, in a dry, cool, ventilated place.
Never store food in containers that held fuel, pesticide or chemicals, and never mix storage chemicals into food meant for home use.

blocks.text: Fair sharing inside the home

In many homes the best pieces of meat or fish go to the father or to guests, and young children eat from a shared bowl with older siblings who eat faster. These customs come from respect and love, but they can leave the people with the highest needs short. Gentle changes work better than arguments: give young children their own plate, set aside the egg or fish for the toddler and the pregnant mother before serving, and explain to the household why.

blocks.title: Be careful with food claims
blocks.text: Messages on WhatsApp often promise that one leaf, tea or powder cures diabetes, cancer or infertility. Treat these as unproven. Varied food supports health but does not replace medical treatment. Check health claims with a health worker or official Ministry of Health and WHO sources before sharing them.

takeaways: Follow the Five Keys: clean, separate, cook, safe temperatures, safe water and food
Cooked food should not sit at room temperature for more than 2 hours
Dry and sort grains and nuts; discard mouldy ones to avoid aflatoxins
Airtight storage controls weevils without chemicals
Serve children and pregnant women deliberately so they get their share

activity.title: Kitchen and store safety check
steps: Walk through your kitchen and food store with the Five Keys list.
Mark each key as done well, partly done or not done.
Do the salt-in-a-bottle test on one stored grain or legume.
Fix the weakest point this week, for example a covered water container or pallets under sacks.
Watch one family meal and note who receives the protein foods.
activity.evidence: Your Five Keys checklist, a photo of the improvement you made, and one note about food sharing

lessons.title: Measuring progress: growth cards, MUAC screening and diet diversity tracking
objectives: Read the direction of a child's growth line on a health card
Interpret a MUAC tape colour and the bilateral oedema check, and refer correctly
Track weekly dietary diversity and calculate averages and percentages
Keep a simple record that shows whether a change is being sustained

blocks.text: A family may feel it is eating better, but feelings can mislead. Health workers rely on a few simple measures. You do not need to diagnose anyone: your role is to keep good records, notice warning signs early, and connect families to the clinic.

blocks.name: growth-chart
blocks.caption: A child's weight line should keep rising in the same direction as the printed curves.

blocks.text: Measure 1: the growth line on the child health card

At immunisation and growth monitoring sessions, clinics weigh children and plot the weight on a chart on the child health card, based on the WHO Child Growth Standards. Read the **direction of the line**, not just one dot. A line rising alongside the printed curves is good. A flat line between two visits, or a line going down, means the child is not growing as expected and needs a health worker's attention and a feeding check, even if the child looks fine. Take the card to every visit and ask the nurse to explain it.
Measure 2: MUAC and the oedema check

MUAC means **mid-upper arm circumference**. A coloured MUAC tape is wrapped around the left upper arm, halfway between the shoulder tip and the elbow, with the arm hanging relaxed. It is used for children aged 6 to 59 months, and many programmes now train mothers to use it themselves. The cut-offs below come from the WHO and UNICEF joint statement on severe acute malnutrition.

head: MUAC reading
Tape colour
Meaning
Action
rows: Refer to a health facility or nutrition treatment site the same day
Take to the clinic for assessment and feeding support; recheck often

blocks.text: Also check for **bilateral pitting oedema**: press your thumbs gently on the top of both feet for 3 seconds. If a dent remains on both feet after you lift your thumbs, the child has oedema, which is a sign of severe acute malnutrition whatever the MUAC reading. Refer at once. In Nigeria, community management of acute malnutrition (CMAM) sites at primary health care centres treat these children, often as outpatients with ready-to-use therapeutic food.

blocks.title: From screening to action
items: Measure MUAC, press both feet
Red or oedema: same-day referral
Yellow: clinic assessment this week
Green: keep feeding, recheck monthly
Record result and follow up
blocks.caption: Screening only helps when every red, yellow or oedema result leads to a clinic visit and a follow-up.

blocks.title: Your role is to refer, not treat
blocks.text: Never give medicines, supplements or therapeutic food on your own, and never tell a family a child is fine because the tape is green if the child looks very ill. Danger signs such as not able to drink, repeated vomiting, convulsions or unusual sleepiness need a health facility immediately.

blocks.title: Worked example: a yellow MUAC result
blocks.context: For example, Fatima, a volunteer in a Zaria women's group, has been trained by the community health worker to use a MUAC tape. She measures 18-month-old Sani's arm at 118 mm and finds no oedema.
steps: 118 mm is between 115 and 124 mm, so the tape shows yellow: moderate acute malnutrition.
She explains calmly to Sani's mother what yellow means and that the clinic can help.
She writes the date, child number, reading (118 mm), oedema (none) and action (referred) in her register.
She agrees with the mother to go to the clinic on its next nutrition day, three days later, and offers to go along.
Two weeks later she visits again and records the new reading.
blocks.result: Sani is assessed and enrolled for feeding support. Fatima's record shows the referral, the visit, and the follow-up reading, so nobody is lost between screening and care.

blocks.text: Measure 3: the weekly diet diversity tracker

For household change, keep a 7-day tracker. Each evening, score the day out of 10 groups for yourself (or out of 8 for a young child). At the end of each week calculate two numbers: the **average score** (total divided by 7) and the **percentage of days that reached the target** (days at 5 or more divided by 7, times 100).

blocks.title: Worked example: four weeks of tracking
blocks.context: For example, Amina from Module 1 started adding ugu, beans and pawpaw. Her daily scores in week 1 were 4, 3, 5, 4, 4, 3, 5. In week 4 they were 6, 5, 5, 6, 7, 5, 6.
steps: Week 1 days at 5 or more: 2. Percentage = 2 / 7 x 100 = about 29%.
Week 4 total: 6 + 5 + 5 + 6 + 7 + 5 + 6 = 40. Average = 40 / 7 = about 5.7.
Week 4 days at 5 or more: 7. Percentage = 7 / 7 x 100 = 100%.
blocks.result: Amina's average rose from 4.0 to 5.7 and she now reaches the target every day. Continuing to track past week 4 will show whether the change lasts through the lean season.

takeaways: Read the direction of a child's growth line; flat or falling needs a health worker
MUAC under 115 mm (red) or oedema of both feet means same-day referral; 115 to 124 mm (yellow) needs clinic assessment
Your role is to screen, record and refer, never to treat
Track weekly diet diversity as an average and a percentage of days on target

activity.title: Start your tracking records
steps: Draw a 7-day diet diversity tracker with columns for each of the 10 groups and a total.
Fill it for one full week and calculate the average and the percentage of days at 5 or more.
Look at the child health card of a child under five in your home and describe the direction of the line.
Find out when your nearest clinic runs growth monitoring or MUAC screening and write it down.
Write who you would call for a red MUAC result, with their phone number.
activity.evidence: Completed weekly tracker with calculations, and your referral contact note

quiz.q: A 4-month-old baby seems thirsty in the hot season. What is the WHO advice?
options: Breastfeed more often; breast milk alone meets the baby's water needs
Give glucose water once a day
quiz.explain: Exclusive breastfeeding for six months means no water or other drinks. Breast milk contains enough water, even in hot weather.

quiz.q: A 10-month-old should usually receive how many meals of complementary food a day?
options: 3 to 4, plus 1 to 2 snacks if hungry
quiz.explain: WHO advises 3 to 4 meals a day from 9 to 23 months, with 1 to 2 snacks, alongside breastfeeding.

quiz.q: Fatima measures a 2-year-old's MUAC at 112 mm. What should happen?
options: Nothing, it is close to normal
Refer to a health facility the same day
Give the child extra pap at home only
quiz.explain: Under 115 mm is red, severe acute malnutrition. The child needs same-day referral.

quiz.q: Stew was cooked at 10 am and left on the table without heat until 3 pm. What is the safe choice?
options: Discard it, because it sat at room temperature for 5 hours
quiz.explain: Cooked food should not stay at room temperature for more than 2 hours. Some bacterial toxins are not destroyed by reheating.

quiz.q: Some groundnuts in a bag are shrivelled and greenish. What should the household do?
options: Roast them well and eat them
Sort out and throw away the damaged nuts, and keep the rest dry
Sell them cheaply at the market
quiz.explain: Mouldy or damaged nuts may contain aflatoxins that cooking does not destroy. Remove and discard them; do not sell or feed them to animals.

quiz.q: Over 7 days a woman's diet scores were 5, 4, 6, 5, 3, 5, 6. What is her average score?

modules.title: Action, Partnerships and Community Impact
modules.overview: You turn what you have learned into lasting change: a kitchen garden and a weekly meal plan at home, then partnerships and clear messages that spread good practice in your community. You finish with a measurable 90-day plan built on your baseline.

lessons.title: From knowledge to action: a kitchen garden and a weekly family meal plan
objectives: Choose one household change that directly closes your identified gap
Set up a small sack or container garden for leafy greens and vitamin A-rich crops
Write a 7-day meal plan and check its food-group coverage
Calculate whether a garden saves money compared with buying

blocks.text: Knowledge only helps when it changes the pot. In Module 1 you wrote one specific gap. Now you will choose one practical change that closes it, start small, and make it a habit. For many families the cheapest lasting change is growing leafy greens at home and planning meals around the food groups.

blocks.name: gardening
blocks.alt: A woman tending plants in a garden
blocks.caption: A few sacks of greens by the door can cover group 7, dark green leafy vegetables, most of the year.

blocks.title: Turning a gap into a habit
items: Name the gap
Pick one change
Plan inputs and cost
Start small this week
Review after four weeks
blocks.caption: One well-chosen change that lasts beats five changes that stop after a fortnight.

blocks.text: Match the change to the gap

head: Gap found in your baseline
Practical change to try
rows: Sack or container garden of ugu, efo tete (amaranth), waterleaf or moringa
Plant orange-fleshed sweet potato vines; buy ripe mango and pawpaw in season; use some red palm oil
Beans or moi moi three times a week; groundnut paste in pap; a few local hens for eggs
Enriched porridge from Module 2, with the child's own plate
Food runs out in the lean months
Buy and store beans and grain after harvest in airtight bags; dry vegetables and fruit in season

blocks.text: Setting up a sack garden

items: Choose a sunny spot near the kitchen door that gets at least half a day of sun and is safe from goats and chickens.
Use strong woven sacks or old buckets with holes punched in the bottom for drainage.
Fill with a mix of good topsoil and well-rotted manure or compost. Put a column of small stones down the middle of large sacks to help water reach the roots.
Plant leafy greens on top and in slits on the sides: efo tete from seed, ugu from its large seeds, waterleaf from stem cuttings.
Water early morning or evening. Rinse water from washing vegetables or rice can be reused, but avoid water with heavy soap or bleach.
Harvest outer leaves regularly so the plant keeps producing; replant a sack every few months.

blocks.title: Get local advice
blocks.text: Your state Agricultural Development Programme (ADP) extension officer, a nearby farmer or a seed seller can tell you which varieties do best in your area and season. Ask before buying seed.

blocks.title: Worked example: does a garden pay?
blocks.context: For example, Kemi in Abeokuta buys a bundle of ugu three times a week for about 500 naira each (approximate). Setup costs (approximate): 4 sacks at 300 naira, topsoil and manure 3,000 naira, seeds and cuttings 2,000 naira.
steps: Current spending on ugu: 3 x 500 = 1,500 naira per week.
Once the sacks are producing enough, the saving is about 1,500 naira per week.
Payback time: 6,200 / 1,500 = about 4 weeks of harvesting.
She also gains fresher leaves picked minutes before cooking, which keeps more vitamin C.
blocks.result: After the first harvests, Kemi's garden pays for itself in about a month and then saves her roughly 6,000 naira a month at these example prices, money she moves to eggs for her toddler.

blocks.text: Eggs from a few hens

A few local hens kept for eggs can give young children a regular source of high quality protein and vitamin A. Eggs are worth more on the child's plate than sold, if the family can manage it. Keep hens in a coop or run, away from the kitchen and the place where babies crawl and play, because contact with animal droppings spreads germs that cause diarrhoea. Wash hands after handling birds or collecting eggs, and cook eggs until the white and yolk are firm.
A 7-day meal plan you can actually follow

Use the meals your family already likes and improve them, rather than inventing new dishes. Write the plan, then count the food groups for each day. The sample below uses common Nigerian meals; the last column counts the 10 groups across the whole day.

head: Day
Morning
Afternoon
Evening
Groups
rows: Rice and beans with ugu stew and fish
Eba with egusi and ugu soup with fish
Jollof rice with okra and fish, banana

blocks.text: Continue the same way for the rest of the week. Rotate protein foods so the family does not tire of them, cook beans in bulk twice a week to save fuel, and plan one market trip around the plan so you buy only what the plan needs. Keep the plan on the wall and tick each meal you actually served.

takeaways: Choose the one change that directly closes your gap
A few sacks of leafy greens can supply group 7 cheaply and pay for themselves
Plan meals the family already enjoys, improved with beans, greens, eggs and fruit
Count food groups per day, aiming for 5 or more
Review after four weeks and keep what works

activity.title: Start one change and one plan
steps: Choose your one change from the table and write why it fits your gap.
Cost it with local prices and calculate any saving or payback time.
Set it up this week: plant the sacks, buy the storage bags or start the enriched porridge.
Write a 7-day meal plan for your household and count the food groups for each day.
Tick the meals you actually serve for one week.
activity.evidence: Photo of your garden or change, the costing, and the ticked 7-day meal plan with daily group counts

lessons.title: Partnerships and communication: clinics, extension workers and cooking demonstrations
objectives: Identify health, agriculture and community partners who can support nutrition work
Write a specific, polite request to a partner
Plan and cost a community cooking demonstration
Share accurate nutrition messages on WhatsApp and in groups

blocks.text: One household can change its own pot. A group of households, working with the clinic and the agriculture office, can change a community. This lesson shows you who to work with, how to ask, and how to share messages people remember and act on.

blocks.name: eating-together
blocks.alt: People sharing a meal around a table
blocks.caption: Cooking and tasting together is one of the most convincing ways to change what families eat.

blocks.text: Who can help

head: Partner
What they can offer
rows: Primary health care centre and community health extension workers (CHEWs)
Growth monitoring, MUAC screening, antenatal care, immunisation, referral for acute malnutrition, accurate health talks
Links between the community and the health facility; can help mobilise households and spaces
State Agricultural Development Programme (ADP) extension officers
Advice on vegetable varieties, seeds and vines, small livestock and post-harvest storage
Women's groups, religious groups, savings groups, PTAs
Regular meetings to reach mothers and fathers; trusted voices
NGOs and development programmes working on nutrition in your state
Training, materials such as MUAC tapes, sometimes seeds or support for demonstrations

blocks.title: Mapping partners by influence and interest
items: High influence, low interest: inform and win over
High influence, high interest: work closely
Low influence, low interest: keep informed
Low influence, high interest: involve as helpers
blocks.caption: Place each partner in a box; spend most time with high-influence, high-interest partners such as the clinic officer in charge.

blocks.text: Ask specifically

Partners respond better to clear requests than to general appeals for help. Say who you are, what you have already done, exactly what you need, and when. Bring your baseline numbers: they show you are serious.

blocks.title: Worked example: a request to the clinic
blocks.context: For example, Grace leads a women's fellowship of 30 members in Makurdi. Her baseline shows 14 children under five in members' homes, and only 4 have been weighed in the last three months.
steps: She visits the primary health care centre and asks to see the officer in charge, rather than leaving a message.
She explains: 'Our fellowship has 14 children under five; only 4 were weighed in the last three months.'
She asks for one thing: 'Could a CHEW do growth monitoring and MUAC screening at our hall after service on a Sunday next month, and give a 15-minute talk on complementary feeding?'
She offers what the group will do: provide the space, a table and chairs, and bring all 14 children with their health cards.
She follows up with a short written note on WhatsApp the same day confirming the date discussed.
blocks.result: The clinic agrees to a date. All 14 children are measured, 2 are referred to the clinic, and the fellowship now has a contact person for future sessions.

blocks.text: Running a cooking demonstration

items: Pick one recipe that fixes the gap you found, such as enriched pap or ugu and bean porridge.
Invite a manageable group, for example 15 mothers and caregivers, and ask a CHEW or experienced cook to co-lead.
Set up a handwashing point with soap and safe water, and follow the Five Keys in front of everyone.
Cook while explaining each ingredient's food group and cost; let participants stir and serve.
Feed the young children present, ask what they liked, and agree on who will try it at home this week.
Follow up a week later: who cooked it, what changed, what was hard.

blocks.text: Costs can be shared. If the ingredients come to about 9,000 naira and firewood or gas about 1,000 naira (approximate), the total of 10,000 naira divided among 15 participants is about 670 naira each. Some groups instead ask each household to bring one ingredient, or seek a local sponsor.
Messages people remember

items: Keep each message to one action: 'Add a spoon of groundnut paste to baby's pap' works better than a lecture on protein.
Show, do not only tell: a photo of the enriched pap or the sack garden is worth a long voice note.
Use local names for foods, and the local language where you can.
Share only from trusted sources: the Federal Ministry of Health, WHO, UNICEF and your clinic. Do not forward miracle cure messages.
Protect privacy: never post a child's MUAC result, photo or name in a group without the parent's clear permission.

blocks.text: Bring fathers and grandmothers in

Mothers usually cook, but fathers often control the money and grandmothers often decide how babies are fed. A message that reaches only mothers may be overruled at home. Invite fathers to a short session at a men's meeting or after prayers, focused on what they can do: give money for eggs and beans, build the garden or coop, and support exclusive breastfeeding. Invite grandmothers to the cooking demonstration and ask for their experience before sharing new advice.

blocks.title: Join forces to buy and store
blocks.text: Several households can pool money to buy beans or grain by the bag soon after harvest, when prices are usually lower, and store it in airtight bags for the lean months. Agree in writing who paid what and how the food will be shared.

takeaways: Clinics, CHEWs, Ward Development Committees and ADP extension officers are your key partners
Make specific requests backed by your baseline numbers
Cooking demonstrations change practice when people cook, taste and follow up
One message, one action, from trusted sources, with privacy respected

activity.title: Make one partnership move
steps: List five possible partners and place each in the influence and interest matrix.
Write a specific request to your top partner using your baseline numbers.
Deliver it in person or by phone, then confirm in writing.
Plan and cost a cooking demonstration for up to 15 people.
Draft three one-action WhatsApp messages with a photo idea for each.
activity.evidence: Partner matrix, your written request and any reply, the demonstration plan with costs, and the three messages

lessons.title: Your household nutrition project and 90-day plan
objectives: Compare your results with your baseline using the same measures
Show evidence that a change has been sustained for several weeks
Write SMART goals and indicators for the next 90 days
Present your project clearly to your family, group or a partner

blocks.text: Your final project brings everything together: the baseline from Module 1, the tools from Module 2 and the actions from Module 3. The aim is not a perfect diet. The aim is a real, measured improvement that your household keeps doing, and a clear plan to extend it.

blocks.name: progress-tracking
blocks.alt: A person reviewing a progress tracker
blocks.caption: Comparing today's numbers with your baseline turns effort into evidence.

blocks.text: Step 1: compare before and after

Use exactly the same measures as at the start, so the comparison is fair: the average dietary diversity score over at least three days, the percentage of days reaching 5 or more groups, the young child's group score out of 8, and, where available, the direction of the child's growth line on the health card. Note what changed, what did not, and why.
Step 2: prove the change lasts

items: Dated photos of the garden at planting, first harvest and four weeks later.
Ticked meal plans for at least three separate weeks.
Your weekly diversity tracker, showing scores held at the new level.
A short note from a family member or the child's caregiver about what is now normal at home.

blocks.text: Step 3: write SMART goals for 90 days

A SMART goal is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. 'Improve nutrition in my street' is not SMART. 'By 31 March, 6 households in my street will reach an average diversity score of 5 or more, measured by 3-day recalls' is SMART.

Each goal needs an **indicator**: the number you will measure, how you will measure it, the baseline and the target. Keep indicators few and simple so you actually collect them. A table like the one below fits on one page and can be shared with a partner.

head: Indicator
How measured
Baseline
Target by day 90
rows: Average dietary diversity score of participating households
Households with producing leafy green sacks
Children under five screened with MUAC
Yellow or red results with a clinic visit within one week

blocks.title: A 90-day plan in four stages
items: Days 1 to 14: baseline and partners
Days 15 to 45: gardens and demonstrations
Days 46 to 75: screening and follow-up
Days 76 to 90: re-measure and report
blocks.caption: Measure at the start and the end with the same tools, and act in between.

blocks.title: Worked example: Bisi's 90-day plan
blocks.context: For example, Bisi in Akure improved her own household's average score from 3.8 to 5.6. She now wants to help 6 neighbouring households. Their baseline averages are 3.5, 4.0, 3.2, 4.6, 3.9 and 4.2.
steps: Households at 5 or more at baseline: 0 of 6, which is 0%.
Goal 1: by day 90, the group average reaches 5.0 and at least 4 of 6 households (67%) average 5 or more.
Goal 2: by day 45, each household has at least 2 producing sacks of leafy greens, checked by photo.
Goal 3: all 9 children under five in the 6 homes are screened with MUAC by a CHEW by day 60, and every yellow or red result has a recorded clinic visit within one week.
She lists her partners: the CHEW at the health centre, an ADP extension officer for vines and seed, and her women's group for a monthly cooking demonstration.
blocks.result: Bisi has three measurable goals, a baseline to compare against, named partners and dates. At day 90 she will repeat the same recalls and report the results to her group and the clinic.

blocks.text: Step 4: share and keep going

Present your results in five minutes: the gap you found, what you changed, the before and after numbers, a photo, and what comes next. Share it with your household, your group and any partner who helped. Thank people by name where they are happy to be named. Then check your seasonal calendar: if the lean months are coming, your next step may be storing beans after harvest or drying leaves while they are plentiful.

Plan for what happens when your energy runs low. Train one or two other women to do the recalls and keep the tracker, so the work does not depend on you alone. Agree a regular slot, such as the first meeting of each month, when the group shares garden harvests, checks the trackers and decides on the next demonstration. Small routines like these are what keep a change alive after the excitement of the first month.

blocks.title: Be honest about results
blocks.text: If a number did not improve, say so and explain what you learned. Honest reports build trust with clinics and funders, and a modest real improvement is worth more than an impressive claim nobody can check.

takeaways: Compare before and after with exactly the same measures
Show the change lasting with dated photos and several weeks of records
Write SMART goals with numbers, dates and named partners
Report honestly and use the seasonal calendar to choose the next step

activity.title: Assemble your project file
steps: Repeat the 3-day recall and calculate your new average and percentage of days at target.
Put the before and after numbers side by side in one table.
Collect your dated photos, ticked meal plans and weekly trackers.
Write three SMART goals for the next 90 days with indicators and partners.
Present the project in five minutes to your household or group and note their feedback.
activity.evidence: Project file with before and after table, evidence of a sustained change, and the written 90-day plan

quiz.q: Kemi's baseline shows her family almost never eats dark green leaves. Which change best fits this gap?
options: Starting a sack garden of ugu and efo tete
quiz.explain: The gap is group 7, dark green leafy vegetables, so growing leafy greens closes it directly.

quiz.q: A garden costs 4,500 naira to set up and saves 900 naira a week once it produces (example figures). How many weeks of harvest to pay back?
Which request to a clinic is most likely to get a useful response?
options: 'Could a CHEW screen our 14 children under five with MUAC at our hall on a Sunday next month? We will bring them with their cards.'
quiz.explain: Specific requests with numbers, a date and an offer of help are easier for partners to say yes to.

options: By day 90, 4 of 6 households will average 5 or more food groups, measured by 3-day recalls
quiz.explain: It is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and has a time limit.

quiz.q: A cooking demonstration costs about 12,000 naira for 15 participants (example figures). If shared equally, how much does each pay?
A member wants to post a child's red MUAC result and photo in the group chat to raise awareness. What should she do?
options: Post it, because awareness is important
Not post it without the parent's clear permission, and focus on getting the child to the clinic
quiz.explain: Children's health information is private. The priority is same-day referral, and nothing should be shared without the parent's permission.

finalQuiz.q: Which statement best describes food security?
options: Having a full store of grain after harvest
All people at all times having access to enough safe, nutritious food for an active, healthy life
finalQuiz.explain: This is the standard FAO definition, covering availability, access, utilisation and stability.

finalQuiz.q: A child is short for his age but not thin. Which form of malnutrition is this most likely?
finalQuiz.explain: Stunting is low height for age and builds up over months of poor diet and illness.

finalQuiz.q: A woman's day included eba, egusi soup with ugu and fish, and a mango. How many of the 10 groups did she eat?
finalQuiz.explain: Grains and roots (eba), nuts and seeds (egusi), dark green leaves (ugu), fish, and vitamin A-rich fruit (ripe mango): 5 groups.

finalQuiz.q: Groundnuts cost 3,000 naira per kg (example price) and contain about 25 g protein per 100 g. What is the cost per gram of protein?
finalQuiz.explain: 1 kg gives about 250 g protein. 3,000 / 250 = 12 naira per gram.

finalQuiz.q: Why should a household draw a seasonal calendar?
options: To see when food runs short, prices rise and illness is common, so action can be timed
To decide when to stop breastfeeding
finalQuiz.explain: The calendar shows the lean months and other pressures, guiding storage, gardens and support.

finalQuiz.q: At what age should complementary foods start, according to WHO?
finalQuiz.explain: Breast milk only for the first 6 months; complementary foods from about 6 months while breastfeeding continues to two years or beyond.

finalQuiz.q: An 8-month-old eats breast milk, pap with groundnut paste and mashed egg. What else would most easily bring her to 5 of 8 groups?
options: Mashed ripe pawpaw or a little ground fish
finalQuiz.explain: She has breast milk, grains, nuts and eggs (4). Pawpaw adds vitamin A-rich fruit or fish adds flesh foods, giving 5.

finalQuiz.q: Which practice follows the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food?
options: Cutting raw chicken and then fruit on the same unwashed board
Leaving stew on the table all afternoon
Reheating stored soup until it is steaming hot and bubbling
Using water from an open pond for baby food
finalQuiz.explain: Reheating thoroughly is part of keeping food at safe temperatures and cooking thoroughly.

finalQuiz.q: What is the safest way to deal with mouldy maize in a store?
options: Remove and throw it away, then dry and store the rest in airtight bags off the floor
finalQuiz.explain: Aflatoxins are not destroyed by cooking. Discard mouldy grain and prevent damp in storage.

finalQuiz.q: A 3-year-old has a MUAC reading of 121 mm and no swelling of the feet. What should a volunteer do?
options: Refer for a clinic assessment and feeding support, and record a follow-up
finalQuiz.explain: 115 to 124 mm is yellow, moderate acute malnutrition. The child should be assessed at the clinic and followed up.

finalQuiz.q: Over a week a household's scores were 5, 5, 4, 6, 5, 3, 5. What percentage of days reached 5 or more?
finalQuiz.explain: 5 of the 7 days scored 5 or more. 5 / 7 x 100 = about 71%.

finalQuiz.q: Which 90-day goal is the most useful for reporting to a clinic partner?
options: By day 60, all 9 children under five in our 6 households are screened with MUAC, and every yellow or red result has a clinic visit within one week
finalQuiz.explain: It is specific, measurable and time-bound, and it links directly to the clinic's work.

capstone.title: Household Nutrition Improvement Project
capstone.brief: Show a measured, sustained nutrition improvement in your own household and a realistic plan to extend it. You submit your baseline, a weekly meal plan using local affordable foods across the food groups, evidence of one change kept up for at least four weeks, before and after diet scores, and a 90-day community plan with SMART goals, indicators and named partners.
steps: Record your baseline: 3-day 24-hour recalls with diversity scores, a seasonal calendar and a community food map.
Name one specific gap (who, what, when) and choose one change that closes it.
Write and follow a 7-day meal plan using local, affordable foods, counting the food groups for each day.
Carry out the change (for example a sack garden, enriched porridge for a young child, or airtight storage) and keep it going for at least four weeks.
Track weekly diversity scores and, for any child under five, note growth card checks or MUAC screening done by a health worker.
Repeat the 3-day recalls and compare before and after with the same measures.
Write a 90-day plan with three SMART goals, an indicator table and at least two partners, and present it to your household or group.
evidence: Baseline sheet with three recall scores per person, seasonal calendar and food map
7-day meal plan with daily food-group counts, ticked for at least three weeks
Dated photos showing the change at start, after two weeks and after four weeks
Weekly diversity tracker with averages and percentage of days on target
Five Keys kitchen checklist with one improvement made
90-day plan with SMART goals, indicator table and named partners
